Core loop

Every tile is an outcome, good or bad

Property

Railroad

Chance

Random card: cash, dice, a free attack

GO

Losses

Income & Luxury Tax

Like a slot reel: mostly wins, with a few losses that make the wins feel earned.

06

Core loop

Two dice make a readable bet

Chance of each total with two six-sided dice

44%

of rolls land 6–8 tiles ahead

Players check how far the next railroad or event tile is before raising the multiplier.

A slot reel hides the next outcome. The board shows it.

Fairness: a Scopely-commissioned review (Trail of Bits, Dec 2024) found the dice generator unbiased.

07

Core loop

The multiplier turns dice into a bet

One tap: ×1 → ×10

Each roll then costs ten dice.

Every payout ×10

Rent, heists, shutdowns and event points.

Regen stops at 40

Rewards can push the count far above it.

08

Core loop

Reward multipliers stack on top

Boosts are timed, so they tell players when to raise the multiplier.

Progression

Cash has one job: 30 builds per board

5 landmarks × 6 stages

Each stage is a cash purchase: “M. Industries 5/30”.

Prices climb per landmark

76.6K → 112K → 140K → 174K on board 5.

Attacks add repair costs

Fixing damage spends cash that would have built.

Progression

Costs outrun income, and dice drops get rarer but bigger

Progression

Net worth unlocks permanent upgrades

Every build raises net worth

Progress that stays

Boards end; the account keeps the upgrades.

14

Family tree

Each part has older roots

1904

The board

The Landlord’s Game led to Parker Brothers’ Monopoly (1935): laps, GO salary, Chance, rent from other players.

Slots

The variable reward

Fruit machines and social-casino slots: spend a credit, get an unpredictable payout, bet more for more.

2009+

The social energy

Facebook-era social games: energy that refills, gifting with friends, and visiting friends’ bases.

Pirate Kings was the first mobile hit to join all three: spin, steal from friends, build.

21

Stealing from friends

Shields soften the hit, they don’t cancel it

The attacker always wins

Two ×10 attacks: blocked paid 150K, a hit paid 360K.

The defender loses nothing

No damage, no repair bill.

Capacity is a reward

The shield cap grows with net worth.

Stealing from friends

The steal is personal: friends hit you most

Friends hit you most

With one friend added, most hits in the log came from them.

Friends pay you rent

“CuteRing45 paying you rent! 189,000.”

It follows you out of the game

Each hit is a push notification naming the friend: an invitation to take revenge.

Live ops & albums

Stickers: a 198-sticker album on a timer

26

Session length

Example sessions

Sessions stretch when everything lines up

One session, by where its dice came from

The multiplier is a fast exit

High stakes burn through dice so a session can end quickly.

…but it scales with your balance

Bigger multipliers only open up with more dice, so every session still gets a minimum number of rolls.

Alignment = +30 minutes

Events, daily rewards and gifts landing together mean half an hour of high-stakes rolling.

27

Session length

Reasons to start another session

Being offline costs you: dice stop refilling at the cap, and friends keep hitting.

28

Session length

Two long-term goals: finish the board, finish the album

Boards: steady and earnable

Every build moves the bar; enough dice always finishes it.

Albums: hard by design

RNG leaves gaps no amount of rolling reliably fills.

Gaps become invites

Trading fills them, so collectors recruit friends to start playing.

32

Results

What Monopoly GO added on top

A well-known IP

  • Monopoly already runs on the same loop: roll, collect, build, charge rent.
  • Same fantasy as the board game: build up, get bankrupted by friends, rebuild.

Seven years, two restarts

  • 7 years of development. It began as a real-time PvP game in the style of Clash Royale.
  • Two versions scrapped: “too competitive” and “too complex”.
  • 2 years spent making board movement fun (LA Times, 2026).

Co-op and stacked events

  • Partner events, tournaments and albums run at once, so every roll does several jobs.
  • 10M people played every day by mid-2024.

Now: community building

  • Official Facebook sticker-trading group, Discord and the Monopoly GO Chat app.
  • VIP programs and community competitions: 12,000 fan entries for one pets contest.
33

Takeaways

At heart, Monopoly GO is a re-imagined slot machine: dice are the spin, the board is the reel, the multiplier is the bet.

01

A proven economy, zero new mechanics

Spin → steal → build → collect, straight from Pirate Kings and Coin Master.

02

One action feeds everything

Every roll pays cash, events, stickers and minigames: the casual-game hallmark.

03

Layered progression

Boards reset, net worth and the album carry forward.

04

Collection is core, not a live-op

The sticker album is always on, not only during events.

05

Sessions flex with the calendar

Live ops and daily rewards lining up turn 5 minutes into 30+.

06

Stealing feels personal

Real names, push alerts and a revenge log give clear reasons to play.

07

A minimal shop

Dice and cash only. Players always know what a dollar buys.

08

Offers at the right moment

Out of dice, on login, near a goal: the offer arrives when it is needed.

09

The IP fits the fantasy

Rent, jail, railroads and Mr. Monopoly already mean what the game needs.

10

High-fidelity polish

Animation, feedback and UX well above typical casual quality.

34

For our game

How this can apply to our game

01

Stealing is toxic, but compelling

Attacks drive return visits and revenge. Use the pull, but cap the pain.

02

Both players can win

Keep a winner, but reward both sides, like the Trick or Treat minigame.

03

Re-skin mechanics

A theme and story over a slot loop makes the old feel new but nostalgic.

04

Make collection core

An always-on collection gives a broad audience a long-term reason to play.

05

Offers that rescue

Show offers only when players need them, framed as solving their problem.

06

Keep it simple

One action, few currencies, obvious goals. Don’t overcomplicate systems.
